entries.name: Granite
entries.notes: The continents' foundation; the game's stone archetype. Slow-cooled deep in the crust, exposed by uplift and erosion.

entries.name: Basalt
entries.weathers_to: deep, fertile clay soils (laterite in the tropics)
entries.notes: The ocean floor's rock and the world's lava-flow rock. Weathers remarkably fast into rich farmland, hence volcanic green belts.

entries.name: Sandstone
entries.notes: Buried beach and dune sands, cemented hard. The orange domes and cliffs of desert country; arches erode from it.

entries.name: Limestone
entries.weathers_to: calcareous soils (terra rossa, rendzina); karst terrain
entries.notes: Made of the dead: compacted shells and coral. Dissolves in rain to make caves, sinkholes and disappearing rivers.

entries.name: Marble
entries.notes: Limestone recrystallised by heat and pressure; veining records warped layers. The white of classical statuary and temples.

entries.name: Slate
entries.notes: Shale squeezed flat until it splits into sheets. Grey-blue, rings when struck, and the classic wet roof of Atlantic coasts.

entries.name: Gneiss
entries.notes: Granite-like rock banded into stripes by deep metamorphism. The deep grey ribs of ancient shields and mountain cores.

entries.name: Quartzite
entries.notes: Sandstone with its grains fused into a single quartz mass; a struck flake sparks. Too hard for easy carving, too poor for soil.

entries.name: Obsidian
entries.notes: Lava frozen too fast to crystallise. Fractures into edges sharper than steel; the sharpest cutting edge known before lasers.

entries.name: Pumice
entries.notes: Frothed lava; light enough to float, so rafts of it drift far downwind and down-current from eruptions. Density is bulk, not solid rock (~2400).

entries.name: Flint
entries.notes: Nodules of silica replacing chalk. The whole arc of human toolmaking, from hand axes to musket embers.

entries.name: Quartz
entries.notes: The most common single mineral at the surface; sand is mostly its grains. Vein quartz often hides the gold.

entries.name: Feldspar (orthoclase)
entries.weathers_to: kaolinite and other clays, silt-sized grus
entries.notes: Half the crust by volume; the salmon-pink crystals in granite. Breaks down into the clays that make porcelain and brick.

entries.name: Calcite (Iceland spar)
entries.notes: The fizz-in-vinegar mineral. Clear crystals split light into two images; sea shells and cave drips are this stuff.

entries.name: Mica (muscovite)
entries.notes: Peels into transparent flexible sheets, the original window glass for stoves and early electrics. Sparkles in wet sand.

entries.name: Talc
entries.notes: Softest mineral on the Mohs scale; greasy feel, scratched by a fingernail. Soapstone carving stone is mostly talc.

entries.name: Graphite
entries.notes: Pure carbon in flaky sheets; conductive, greasy, leaves a black streak. Named from the Greek for writing.

entries.name: Halite (rock salt)
entries.weathers_to: dissolves in water; salt collapse features
entries.notes: A vanished sea, crystallised. Domes of it pierce up through the other sediments and trap oil beside them.

entries.name: Gypsum
entries.weathers_to: dissolves slowly; lenticular sand desert crusts
entries.notes: Scratch it with a fingernail; bake the powder and it sets as plaster of Paris. Desert roses are this.

entries.name: Kaolinite (china clay)
entries.notes: Feldspar rotted all the way down by warm rain over millions of years. The basis of porcelain and glossy paper.

entries.name: Pyrite
entries.weathers_to: acid mine drainage; limonite (iron oxide) gossan
entries.notes: Fool's gold that sparks: cubic brass-yellow crystals. Where it oxidises it sours streams; where it sits with gold it points the way.

entries.name: Coal (bituminous)
entries.weathers_to: oxidises slowly; coal dust and iron stains
entries.notes: Carboniferous swamp forests, pressed for 300 million years. Black, glossy, streaks brown; the reason steel is cheap.

entries.name: Hematite
entries.notes: The red streak betrays it. Most of the world's iron comes from 2.5-billion-year-old banded iron formations.

entries.name: Magnetite
entries.notes: Naturally magnetic iron ore; lodestone, the first compass needle. Sands blackened by it concentrate the world's iron.

entries.name: Chalcopyrite
entries.notes: Brassy yellow, softer than pyrite; the workhorse of porphyry copper deposits, the greatest holes humans dig.

entries.name: Native copper
entries.weathers_to: green and blue copper carbonates (malachite, azurite)
entries.notes: Copper you can hammer straight out of a rock; the Keweenaw peninsula supplied the old world for six thousand years.

entries.name: Malachite
entries.notes: Banded green crusts over copper deposits; where you see it, copper is near. Dust is toxic: handle specimens with care.

entries.name: Bauxite
entries.notes: Not a single mineral but the residue of tropical rain leaching everything else from rock. Shallow, red, pisolitic (pea-gravel texture).

entries.name: Galena
uses: primary lead ore (car batteries, radiation shielding)
entries.notes: Heavy, bright cubic cleavage mirrors; fresh cleavage flashes like metal. Main ore of lead and a major silver source.

entries.name: Sphalerite
entries.notes: Resinous brown to black; looks nothing like zinc until roasted. Almost every zinc object traces back to this crystal.

entries.name: Cassiterite
entries.notes: Dark, heavy, brown-black; washed down from tin granites into stream gravels. Cornwall's tin fed the Bronze Age.

entries.name: Native gold
entries.weathers_to: native grains in placer river gravels
entries.notes: So dense it stays put while rock washes away: pan every bend of a gold river. Nearly incorruptible; pirates' and banks' metal.

entries.name: Native silver
entries.notes: Rarely found as pure wires and leaves; most silver comes as a byproduct of lead, zinc and copper ores.

entries.name: Native sulfur
entries.weathers_to: sulfuric acid in groundwater when oxidised
entries.notes: Yellow crusts around volcanic vents and salt domes; smell matches the pit. Half the world's sulfuric acid starts here or in the gas it comes with.

entries.name: Cinnabar
entries.notes: Vermilion red, dense, toxic dust. Almadén in Spain mined it for two thousand years; boiling it off yields quicksilver.

entries.name: Diamond
entries.notes: Grows 150 to 250 km down in the mantle; only volcanic kimberlite pipes hurl it to the surface. Digging it up is a lottery of one pipe in a thousand.

entries.name: Corundum (ruby and sapphire)
entries.weathers_to: very resistant; concentrates in placer gravels
entries.notes: Second-hardest natural material; ruby is red corundum (chromium), sapphire everything else. Sri Lanka and Myanmar host the classic deposits.

entries.name: Emerald (beryl)
entries.notes: Beryl coloured by a whisper of chromium. Colombia's Muzo mines set the standard; flawless stones are vanishingly rare, flaws included in the price.

entries.name: Opal
entries.weathers_to: dehydrates to chalcedony or chert over long times
entries.notes: Silica and water; the play-of-colour is light diffracted through ordered spheres of it. Australia's outback fields supply ~95% of the world's opal.

entries.name: Pitchblende (uraninite)
entries.notes: Black, heavy, greasy-looking and faintly radioactive; Curie extracted radium from tons of it. Pure uraninite crystals run about 10650 kg/m3; massive pitchblende runs lighter.
